analysis.one_liner: Forces pharmacy middlemen to pass negotiated drug rebates to insurers and show discounts at the counter.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to make pharmacy benefit managers disclose and pass along drug rebates died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets pharmacy benefit managers, the middlemen that negotiate drug prices between insurers, drugmakers, and pharmacies. It would require PBMs to pass a minimum share of the rebates they negotiate to the insurers and employers that sponsor drug plans, and to show negotiated discounts at the pharmacy counter for Medicare Part D drugs for five years, so patients pay the discounted price when they fill a prescription. It would also publish each PBM's rebate and pass-through numbers on a public federal website, ban contingent pharmacy fee clawbacks during the same five-year window, and give pharmacies a way to appeal reimbursements that fall below their actual costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Part D enrollees, who would see negotiated discounts at the pharmacy counter instead of paying the sticker price; employers and other plan sponsors, who would receive a minimum share of the rebates PBMs now partly keep; and pharmacies, which would stop losing money to contingent fees and could appeal below-cost reimbursement. Patients and employers could also compare PBMs on a public website.

how_it_helps.text: PBMs must pass a minimum share of negotiated rebates and discounts to plan sponsors, with the percentage set by the Health and Human Services Secretary to give patients the maximum benefit.

For plan years 2021 through 2025, negotiated prices for Medicare Part D drugs must be provided at the point of sale, so the discount shows up when the patient fills the prescription rather than later or not at all.

Starting in 2020, the Health and Human Services Department must post each PBM's rebates, discounts, and pass-through amounts on a public website so patients and employers can compare PBMs, displayed in aggregate so no single drug or plan is identified.

For 2021 through 2025, contingent pharmacy price concessions are frozen, and pharmacies get a written appeal process through the Medicare ombudsman if they are reimbursed below their actual cost to acquire and dispense a drug.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers, the three-firm middlemen industry between drugmakers, insurers, and pharmacies, would lose part of the rebate spread they keep and face public disclosure of their performance. Many PBMs are owned by large health insurers, so those parent companies would absorb the loss. Insurers and plan sponsors would bear the cost of new compliance, audit, and claim-disclosure requirements, which could flow into premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their parent insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill never touches drugmakers' list prices; it works only through intermediaries, so manufacturers keep setting prices and can raise them to offset larger rebate pass-throughs.

The point-of-sale freeze and the ban on contingent pharmacy fees last only through 2025; after that, PBMs can apply price concessions again as long as they are tied to quality measures the Secretary approves.

The required minimum pass-through is set 'taking into account the costs of negotiating' rebates, so PBMs can still keep a cut, and new compliance and reporting costs on plans and PBMs could be passed to consumers through premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are real but modest: patients at the pharmacy counter, employers footing drug bills, and pharmacies squeezed by contingent fees all come out ahead, while the cost falls on a middleman industry that keeps a share of negotiated savings today. The design is honest about its limits — it does not cap drug prices, lets PBMs keep some of the spread to cover negotiating costs, and sunsets its strongest protections after five years — but on balance the benefits go to consumers and the costs to concentrated industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator John Kennedy introduced the bill on July 24, 2019 with eleven cosponsors from both parties — 3 Democrats and 8 Republicans, including senators from red and blue states alike.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and the large insurers that own them are better off, because the rebate pass-through mandate, public disclosure, point-of-sale pricing, and pharmacy protections never took effect. Medicare patients and pharmacies, the bill's intended beneficiaries, gained nothing from the two-year run.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy middlemen and their parent insurers

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship split 8 Republicans and 3 Democrats, but because the bill never got a committee markup or floor vote, no roll calls exist to measure the split.

industries.note: PBMs must pass a minimum share of negotiated rebates to plan sponsors, post their rebate and pass-through performance on a public website, and deliver Part D discounts at the point of sale for five years — shrinking the spread they keep today and ending contingent pharmacy fee clawbacks during that window. Patients and employers currently pay the difference through higher copays and plan costs.

The bill freezes contingent pharmacy price concessions for 2021–2025, requires line-item disclosure of every fee and adjustment on each claim, and lets pharmacies appeal reimbursements below their actual acquisition and dispensing costs. This protects the pharmacies patients actually use, many of which lose money on certain prescriptions today.

industries.industry: Health insurers and Medicare Part D plan sponsors
industries.note: Plan sponsors receive a minimum share of negotiated rebates and gain the right to bar noncompliant PBMs from their contracts, which could lower plan costs and premiums. Since several large PBMs are owned by insurers, part of the benefit stays inside the same corporate family.

Manufacturers' negotiated discounts become publicly visible through the required PBM disclosures, though only in aggregate, so individual drug pricing stays confidential. The bill leaves their list prices untouched.
